title: A safe database failover
summary: Quorum, fencing, promotion and redirection.

steps.n: Several health checks fail, and the group votes on whether the primary is really down.
A majority agrees, which avoids acting on one lost network packet.
The old primary is cut off so it cannot accept writes if it comes back.
The most up-to-date replica is chosen to limit lost commits.
The replica stops replaying and becomes the new primary.
A proxy, virtual address or DNS change sends clients to the new primary, and connections reconnect.

title: Why a connection pooler helps
summary: Many clients sharing a few database connections.

steps.n: Each application instance opens its pool to the pooler instead of the database.
The pooler keeps a small set of server connections open to the database.
A client sends a transaction and the pooler assigns it a free server connection.
When the transaction ends, the server connection returns to the pool for another client.
The database sees a steady, small number of sessions and keeps memory for queries.
Monitoring shows clients waiting for a connection, which tells you when to tune or scale.

title: How Ansible finds the hosts to change
summary: From an inventory file and a group name to a list of machines.

steps.l: Run a play against a group
steps.n: The engineer runs a playbook that says hosts: web. Ansible must now work out which machines belong to web.
The control node reads the inventory file or script, where machines are listed and put into groups.
The inventory returns every host in web, including hosts that are in child groups of web.
Group variables and host variables are collected, and the more specific host value wins over the group value.
The control node opens an SSH connection to every host in the list, a few at a time (the forks setting).
Each host returns ok, changed, failed or unreachable, and the run summary counts them per host.

title: Why running a playbook twice is safe
summary: A module checks the current state before it changes anything.

steps.n: The task says a package must be present or a line must exist in a file. It describes the end state, not the steps.
The module looks at the host: is the package installed, does the line already exist?
On the second run the host already looks as requested, so there is nothing to do.
The module reports ok and changes nothing, so the summary shows changed=0 for that task.

steps.l: State differs on a new host
steps.n: On a different host the package is missing, so the module installs it.
That host is reported as changed. Counting changed tasks tells you whether a second run found drift.

title: Which variable value wins
summary: Several places define the same variable, and Ansible has a fixed order.

steps.n: A role ships a default value, designed to be the easiest thing to override. It has very low priority.
A value set for the group in the inventory replaces the role default for all hosts in that group.
A value set for one host is more specific, so it replaces the group value on that machine only.
A value passed with -e on the command line beats everything else, which makes it handy and risky.
The task sees one value. When it is not the one you expected, run with -vvv or use the debug module.
Define each variable in as few places as you can, so the answer to which value wins is obvious.

title: Turning a template into a config file
summary: Facts and variables are merged into a Jinja2 template on the control node.

steps.n: The control node collects facts such as the host name, addresses and memory from the target.
Facts are joined with inventory and role variables to build the data that the template can use.
The template is a normal file with placeholders such as a listen port and a loop over backend servers.
Jinja2 replaces the placeholders and runs the loops, producing the final text on the control node.
The template module compares the rendered text with the file on the host and writes it only if different.
When the file changed, the task notifies a handler so the service reloads once at the end.

title: What happens when a role is applied
summary: A role bundles tasks, defaults, templates and handlers behind one name.

steps.n: The playbook lists roles: [nginx]. Ansible looks for the role folder in the roles path or a collection.
The role defaults load first as low priority variables, so users of the role can change them.
The tasks in tasks/main.yml are added to the play in order, with the role variables available.
Each task runs on the target host. Templates and files come from the role's own folders.
Tasks that changed something notify handlers. Handlers run after the tasks of the play.
The handler runs one time, even if five tasks notified it, and the service picks up the new config.

title: Previewing a change with check mode
summary: Check mode and diff show what would change without changing it.

steps.n: The engineer adds the two flags to the normal command. Nothing will be written to the hosts.

steps.l: Ask each module what it would do
steps.n: Modules that support check mode compare the desired state with the real state and only report.
The host answers with changed or ok, and for files the diff of old and new content.
The engineer reads exactly which lines would be added or removed on which hosts.
A colleague checks the diff. Surprises here are cheap, because nothing has been changed yet.
After approval the same command runs without --check. Tasks that cannot preview, such as shell commands, still need care.

title: Debugging a failed run step by step
summary: From a vague error to the line that explains it.

steps.n: The output names the task, the host and the error message. Start with the first failure, not the last.
Running again with -vvv shows the exact arguments and the connection details used for the task.
If the host is unreachable, test SSH by hand with the same user and key to separate network from Ansible.
A debug task prints the variable the module receives, which often exposes a wrong or empty value.
Use --limit for one host and --start-at-task to repeat only the failing part of the run.
After the fix, run the whole play again. Because tasks are idempotent, the earlier steps report ok.

title: Installing and using a collection
summary: How modules from a collection reach your playbook.

steps.n: The requirements file names each collection and a version range, so every engineer gets the same set.
ansible-galaxy collection install fetches the packages from the configured source.
The collections are unpacked into a folder that Ansible searches for modules, roles and plugins.
The playbook calls a module by its full name, such as community.general.ufw, so there is no doubt where it comes from.
Ansible loads the module code from the collection and runs it like any built-in module.
Pinning versions in the requirements file means an update is a reviewed change, not a surprise.

title: How an index speeds up a query
summary: A lookup that walks a tree instead of reading every row.

steps.n: The application asks for the orders of customer 42. The planner decides how to find them.
Without an index the database would read every row and test each one, which is slow on a large table.
An index on customer_id is a sorted structure, so the planner picks it when few rows match.
The database descends a few levels of the tree to find the entries for customer 42.
The index entries point to the rows, and only those rows are read from the table.
The answer comes back in milliseconds. The cost is that every insert and update must also maintain the index.

title: Reading a query plan
summary: What EXPLAIN tells you before you change anything.

steps.n: The engineer asks the database how it would run the query, without necessarily running it.
The planner uses table statistics to estimate rows and cost for each possible way of running the query.
The plan lists steps such as a sequential scan, an index scan and a join method, with row estimates.
The most nested step runs first. Look for a scan on a big table that returns few rows.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and shows actual rows. A big gap suggests stale statistics.
Add an index or rewrite the query, then explain again. Keep the change only if the plan really improved.

title: Readers and writers without waiting
summary: Multi-version concurrency lets a reader see a steady snapshot.

steps.n: The reader gets a snapshot, which means it sees only data committed before it started.
The writer does not overwrite the row. It creates a new version and marks the old one as replaced.

steps.l: Reader still sees the old version
steps.n: The reader keeps reading the old version, so it is not blocked and sees consistent data.
The commit is recorded. New transactions will now see the new version of the row.
When the reader ends, old versions that nobody needs any more can be removed.
A background process (vacuum in some databases) removes them. Very long transactions delay this cleanup.

title: How a deadlock happens and resolves
summary: Two transactions wait for each other until one is cancelled.

steps.n: Transaction A updates row 1 and holds a lock on it until it commits.
Transaction B updates row 2 and holds that lock.
A now needs row 2, which B holds, so A waits.
B needs row 1, which A holds. Both are now waiting for each other and neither can continue.
The lock manager notices the circular wait after a short timeout.
One transaction is rolled back with a deadlock error, and the other can finish. The application should retry the cancelled one.

title: Why a replica can show old data
summary: Replication copies changes after the primary has committed them.

steps.n: The application saves an order. The primary commits it and returns success.
The change is written to a log and streamed to replicas. This takes some time.

steps.l: Read from the replica at once
steps.n: The application immediately reads the order from a replica to spread the load.
The replica has not applied the change yet, so the order seems missing. This is replica lag.
The change arrives and is applied. A moment later the same read would succeed.
Send reads that must see a fresh write to the primary, or wait until the replica reports the matching position.

title: Changing a column without downtime
summary: The expand and contract pattern in small safe releases.

steps.n: The engineer adds a nullable column. The old application ignores it, so nothing breaks.
The new release writes to the old and the new column, and still reads from the old one.
A script copies old values into the new column in small batches, avoiding long locks.
The next release reads from the new column. If something is wrong, you can go back.

steps.l: Contract: stop writing the old one
steps.n: After a safe period the code stops writing the old column.
Only now is the old column removed. Each step could be rolled back until this one.

title: The cache-aside pattern
summary: Check the cache first, fall back to the database, and fill the cache.

steps.n: The application asks the cache for the product with a key such as product:42.
The cache does not have it, because it expired or was never loaded.
The application reads the product from the database, the source of truth.
The database answers, which costs far more time than a cache read.
The application writes the value into the cache with a time to live, so stale data cannot stay forever.
The next request finds the value in the cache and never touches the database. After an update, delete the cache key.

title: Proving a backup can be restored
summary: A backup is only real once a restore has worked.

steps.n: The scheduler creates a base backup and keeps the log files, on storage separate from the database server.
The job records size, duration and a checksum so that a sudden change gets noticed.
On a schedule, a test server restores the latest backup and replays logs up to a chosen time.
The checker counts rows in key tables, runs a few known queries and compares them with expected values.
A failed restore raises an alert the same day, not on the day of the real disaster.
The restore time becomes a real number for your recovery objective, instead of a guess.

title: How a service log reaches journalctl
summary: From a program writing a line to you reading it.

steps.n: The service just prints a line. Under systemd, standard output and error are connected to the journal.
The journal attaches the unit name, process id, time and priority to the line.
Entries are stored in a binary log, in memory only or on disk depending on the configuration.
The engineer asks for one unit. Filters such as --since and -p err narrow the answer.
Matching entries come back in time order, and -f keeps following new ones.
Size and age limits remove old entries, so a noisy service cannot fill the disk.

title: What happens when you run sudo
summary: A rule lookup, a password check and a logged command.

steps.n: The user prefixes the command with sudo. The sudo program is installed with the setuid bit, so it starts as root.
sudo reads /etc/sudoers and its include files to see whether this user may run this command as root.
A matching rule allows it, perhaps without a password. No rule means the attempt is refused.
If a password is needed, sudo asks for the caller's own password, not the root password.
With permission granted, sudo starts the command with root rights for that one command.
Every use is written to the auth log with the user, the command and the result, which makes review possible.

title: Where output goes: stdout, stderr and redirects
summary: Two streams, and how the shell wires them to files.

steps.n: A command writes its results to standard output, file descriptor 1.
The same command writes errors to standard error, file descriptor 2, even though both usually appear on screen.
By default both streams are connected to the terminal, so you see them mixed.
Writing 'cmd > out.log' sends only standard output to the file. Errors still appear on the terminal.
Writing 'cmd > out.log 2>&1' sends errors to the same place as standard output. The order matters.
Sending only results to a file and keeping errors on the terminal is often the most useful setup for scripts.

title: Reading a file line by line
summary: How while read processes input one record at a time.

steps.l: Redirect the file into the loop
steps.n: 'done < file' attaches the file to the loop's standard input.
The read builtin takes a line from standard input and returns success while lines remain.
With IFS set, the line is split into the named variables. The last variable gets the rest of the line.
The body uses the variables, for example to call a command for each user name in the file.
When the body finishes, the loop reads the next line.
At end of file, read returns failure and the loop ends. A last line without a newline needs extra care.

title: What pip does inside a virtual environment
summary: Packages are installed next to the project, not into the system.

steps.n: python3 -m venv .venv makes a private folder with its own interpreter and site-packages.
Activation puts the venv bin folder first in PATH, so python and pip refer to the private copies.
pip install -r requirements.txt reads the list of packages and versions.
pip finds versions that satisfy all requirements and downloads wheels from the index.
The packages go into the venv, so the system Python stays clean and other projects are unaffected.
The project imports what it needs from the venv. Delete the folder and rebuild when things get confusing.

title: How an exception travels up the call stack
summary: Raise, propagate, catch and clean up.

steps.n: main calls load_config, which is a normal function call that adds a frame to the stack.
load_config calls open on a path that does not exist.
The error is raised. The current function stops running at that line.
load_config has no handler, so the exception moves to its caller, main. Frames are removed as it goes.
main has try/except FileNotFoundError and the handler runs, where it can print a clear message.
The handler logs the cause and exits with a non-zero code. A finally block would run on every path.

title: How a machine finds a neighbour's hardware address
summary: ARP maps an IP address to a MAC address on the local network.

steps.n: Host A wants to reach 10.0.0.20 on the same network, so it must send the frame straight to that machine.
A checks its cache for a recent mapping of that address. If it exists, the lookup ends here.
Who has 10.0.0.20? is sent to every device on the local network.
The switch floods the broadcast, and every host sees it but only the owner of the address answers.
Host B answers directly to A with its hardware address.
A stores the mapping for a short time and sends the data frame to B's MAC.

title: How NAT lets a private host reach the internet
summary: Source address rewriting and the translation table.

steps.n: A host at 192.168.1.10 sends a packet to a public server. Its source address is private and not routable.
The router records the private address and port against a new public port.
The packet leaves with the router's public address as the source.
The server answers to the router's public address and the chosen port.
The router finds which private host and port belong to that public port.
The destination is changed back and the reply reaches the host. Unrequested inbound traffic has no entry and is dropped.

title: How image layers and the container layer work
summary: Shared read-only layers plus one thin writable layer.

steps.n: Each instruction in the build adds a read-only layer. Unchanged layers are reused from the cache.
The container uses all image layers together as one read-only filesystem.
A thin layer is placed on top for anything the container changes.
Changing an existing file copies it into the writable layer first. The image layer stays untouched.
A second container from the same image reuses the same layers, so it starts quickly and uses little disk.
Removing the container deletes its writable layer. Data that must stay belongs in a volume.

title: Pushing an image to a registry
summary: Tags, digests and which layers are uploaded.

steps.n: docker tag adds a name that includes the registry address, the repository and a version tag.
The engine starts uploading the image to that address after logging in.
For each layer the engine checks if the registry already has it, and skips those that do.
Only new layers travel over the network, which makes repeated pushes fast.
The registry stores the manifest and returns a digest, a hash that identifies exactly this image.
A node pulls using the digest. Tags can move, but a digest always points to the same content.

title: Building once and promoting the same artifact
summary: Why staging and production run the identical build.

steps.n: The pipeline compiles the code and packages it exactly once for this commit.
The package is saved with a version and a checksum, so it can be found and verified later.
Staging pulls that same artifact and runs integration tests against it.
Results are recorded against the artifact version, not against a branch that might have moved.
After approval production pulls the identical artifact. Nothing is rebuilt.
The running version maps back to one commit and one test record, which makes rollback and audit simple.

title: A deploy gate with approval
summary: Automatic checks first, then a person for risky changes.

steps.n: Tests, security scans and policy rules run first. Failing any of them stops the pipeline.
All checks are green, and the result is attached to the release.
A production deploy waits for an approver. The request shows the change, the test results and the risk.
The approver should be someone other than the author, who decides after reading the evidence.
The pipeline deploys with the rollout strategy defined for the service, such as canary then full.
Health checks decide whether the release is kept. The approval, the time and the version are stored for audit.

title: How an ingress terminates TLS
summary: From a browser request to a pod, with the certificate handled at the edge.

steps.n: The browser opens a connection to the cloud load balancer that fronts the cluster.
The load balancer forwards the connection to ingress controller pods inside the cluster.
The controller picks the certificate from a secret that matches the host name and completes the TLS handshake.
It decrypts the request and checks host and path against the ingress rules.
The request goes to the service named in the matching rule.
The service sends it to one of the ready pods, which answers over plain HTTP inside the cluster.

title: How a Job and a CronJob run to completion
summary: Unlike a Deployment, a Job is meant to finish.

steps.n: At the scheduled time the CronJob creates a Job object, unless the previous run is still going and the policy forbids it.
The Job controller creates a pod that runs the task once.
The container runs its command and exits with a status code.
Exit status 0 marks the pod succeeded. Any other status marks it failed.
On failure the controller creates a new pod, up to the backoff limit, with growing delays.
When the required number of pods succeed, the Job completes. Old Jobs are removed by the history limits.

title: Why for_each is safer than count
summary: Removing an item from the middle of a list.

steps.l: Start with count over a list
steps.n: Three servers are created with count and a list of names. State addresses them as [0], [1] and [2].
The list shrinks to two names, so the item that was at index 2 moves to index 1.
Terraform sees that [1] now has a different name and [2] is gone.
It plans to change or destroy servers that nobody meant to touch, only because positions shifted.

steps.l: Use for_each with a set or map
steps.n: Each server is addressed by its key, such as web-b, so the address is stable.

steps.l: Only the removed one is destroyed
steps.n: The plan now destroys exactly the removed key and leaves the others alone.

title: Separate environments with separate state
summary: Why dev and prod must not share a state file.

steps.n: The engineer runs plan with the dev settings. It reads the dev state and the dev account only.
Changes go to the dev account, and only the dev state is updated.
The same code runs with different variable files, so the shape matches and only the sizes differ.
The same code is planned against the prod state and the prod account, usually by a pipeline with an approval step.
Prod changes happen only after the change was proven in dev. A mistake in dev cannot reach the prod state.
Separate credentials and state locations mean most people can change dev but not prod.

title: How a cloud load balancer removes a broken server
summary: Health checks and draining.

steps.n: The load balancer sends a health request to every target every few seconds.
Both targets answer with success, so both receive traffic.
Clients send requests and the balancer spreads them across healthy targets.
A deploy breaks the health endpoint on server A, which now returns errors.
After a few failed probes in a row the balancer stops sending new requests to A.
Server B carries the load. Capacity and alerts matter here, because one server is now doing the work of two.

title: Fetching a secret at run time
summary: The application asks for the secret with its own identity.

steps.n: The workload runs with an identity assigned by the platform, so no password is stored in its image.
The application asks the secrets service for db/password.
The service checks that this role is allowed to read exactly this secret.
The secret is returned over an encrypted connection and kept in memory.
Who read which secret and when is written to the audit log.
The service creates a new value on a schedule. Applications that fetch at start-up or refresh periodically pick it up.

title: How an alert reaches the right person
summary: Rules, grouping, routing and silence.

steps.n: The rule runs every minute against the metrics, for example error ratio above 5 percent for 10 minutes.
When the condition holds long enough, the alert is sent with labels such as service and severity.
Alerts with the same labels are grouped, so one outage does not create fifty messages.
Low severity goes to a channel for working hours.
High severity pages the person on call, using the schedule, with a link to the dashboard and runbook.
When the condition clears a resolved message is sent. A silence mutes planned work.

title: From request logs to an SLO number
summary: How raw events become one reliability figure.

steps.n: Each request increments a counter labelled with its status code and route.
The SLI is the share of good requests: non-5xx responses divided by all valid requests.
The query computes this ratio over 30 days and also over short windows for alerting.
The result is compared with the SLO, for example 99.9 percent.
The remaining budget is the allowed bad fraction minus the actual bad fraction, shown as minutes or requests.
With budget left the team ships. With it nearly spent, the team focuses on reliability work.

title: Running a blameless review
summary: Learning from an incident without pointing fingers.

steps.n: The facilitator brings in responders, owners of affected systems and anyone who made a decision.
Using chat logs and graphs, the group writes what happened and when, with facts only.
Questions focus on what made the action seem reasonable at that moment and what information was missing.
The group lists conditions such as missing alerts, unclear runbooks or risky defaults. There is rarely one root cause.
Each action has an owner, a date and a measurable outcome. Fewer, stronger actions beat a long list.
The review is shared widely and the actions are tracked until done, which is how trust in the process is earned.

title: Planning capacity before it runs out
summary: Forecasting from growth and headroom.

steps.n: Weeks of data on traffic, CPU, memory and storage show the growth rate and the daily peaks.
The forecast extends the trend, adds known events such as a launch, and shows when the limit is reached.
The plan keeps a safety margin, so the loss of a zone or a traffic spike does not cause an outage.
Autoscaling handles fast changes. Slow resources such as storage or quota increases need lead time.
A load test shows if the system really scales as predicted, and where the next bottleneck is.
Forecasts are compared with reality each quarter, and the model is corrected where it was wrong.
